title: why the symbol is an execution device
hook: why the symbol is an execution device
carry: the worst thing is not the last thing
tomorrow: the women went to the tomb first

segments.voice: Two weeks. Say the second week's words with me, fast. Deliver us. The Sabbath. The Good Samaritan. The Prodigal Son. The Beatitudes. Love, the kind you do when you don't feel it. And today, the hardest one. Day fourteen.

Look around almost any town and you'll see it. On a steeple. On a necklace. Tattooed on a forearm. Hanging from a rearview mirror. The cross may be the most recognized symbol on earth. Now try something. Imagine a movement whose symbol was an electric chair. A tiny gold noose on a chain. It sounds unthinkable. But that's what the cross was to the people who first saw it. Not a decoration. The way Rome killed the people it wanted everyone to watch die. So why would anyone wear one? Today's word.
screen: `ON A STEEPLE. ON A NECKLACE.` → `IMAGINE AN ELECTRIC CHAIR.` → `WHY WOULD ANYONE WEAR ONE?`

segments.voice: The cross. Crucifixion was how Rome executed slaves, rebels and anyone it saw as a threat to order. It was slow, and it was public on purpose: by the roads, where people would see it and learn. The Gospels say Jesus was arrested at night, questioned, and handed to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, who sentenced him. Roman soldiers carried it out. Over his head they nailed the charge: the King of the Jews. A mockery, and a warning. The Gospels keep a few things he said there. In Luke: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." In Mark, he cries out in Aramaic, his own language, the first line of an old psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" The Gospels don't smooth that over. Many Christians say it's there so that anyone who has felt abandoned knows he felt it too. Here's the surprise. For the first few centuries, Christians mostly drew other signs: a fish, an anchor, a shepherd. The cross became the main symbol later, after Rome stopped crucifying people. But the idea was there from the start. Paul wrote that he had decided to know nothing among them "save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." Christians say something happened there that changed what the worst thing means. Churches put it in different words: a sacrifice, a rescue, love going all the way down. And they show it differently. Catholic and Orthodox churches often show the crucifix, with Jesus on it. Many Protestant churches show the cross empty. Both are saying something about that Friday: it happened, and Christians say it wasn't the end.
screen: `ROME'S PUBLIC EXECUTION.` · `"FATHER, FORGIVE THEM."` · `FIRST A FISH, AN ANCHOR.` · `THE CRUCIFIX AND THE EMPTY CROSS.` · then, large: `IT WASN'T THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe out. Think of a hard thing from this year. Not the hardest. Just name it, quietly, without reliving it. Now notice one plain fact: you're still here. Something came after it, even if it's only this minute, sitting and breathing. You don't have to make it mean anything. Just hold both: it happened, and it wasn't the last thing. If you pray, you can bring it with you. Forty-five seconds. The bell holds the time.
The cross. Rome's execution, turned into the most recognized sign on earth. Fourteenth word. Two weeks.
screen: `THE CROSS — your 14th word` → the strand, fourteen lit → `WEEK TWO. DONE.`

segments.voice: Your line: the worst thing is not the last thing. Today, when something goes wrong, say it to yourself once. Week three is the last in this camp: a morning at a tomb, songs that shout, a seed, a whisper, a table and the people around it. Day fourteen.

howItsDone: Christians remember the crucifixion on Good Friday, the Friday before Easter. Many make the sign of the cross when they pray, and many churches hold a crucifix or a plain cross at the front.

what it means: Rome's public execution, which Christians made the center of their faith.
what a scholar hears: early Christians mostly drew a fish or an anchor. the cross became the main sign in the 300s, after Rome stopped crucifying people.

notes: Rome executed Jesus: the script names Pilate and Roman soldiers and avoids any deicide framing. Keep it that way in any edit.

'The cross became the main symbol later, after Rome stopped crucifying people' (Constantine, 4th century) is the common scholarly account but simplified; confirm the phrasing, and that early crosses do appear in some sources.
Different understandings of the cross (sacrifice, rescue, love) are named without choosing one; a Keeper may prefer different wording.
Crucifix vs empty cross described as 'often' and 'many'; some Protestant churches (e.g. Lutheran) also use crucifixes.
